Chapter 7: The Practice of Presence—Experiencing God in Daily Life.
You know, for a lot of people, the idea of actually experiencing God can feel way out of reach. Like it’s only possible for saints, mystics, or those with a rock-solid faith. But if you listen to the stories that unfold in the therapy room, something different comes to light. God’s presence isn’t locked away on mountaintops or hidden in dramatic miracles. More often, it shows up in the simple, ordinary rhythms that make up our daily lives.
Picture this: a mother, completely overwhelmed by work and family, finds herself folding laundry at the end of a long day. Suddenly, she’s wrapped in a quiet sense of peace. The chaos fades, and for just a moment, she feels held—like she isn’t alone after all. It wasn’t flashy or dramatic, but it was real. That was presence.
Or imagine a man, struggling with loneliness after a painful breakup. He starts noticing little moments of grace—a stranger’s kind word, the warmth of sunlight on his skin, the comfort of a favorite song on the radio. These moments don’t erase the pain. But they offer tiny glimpses of hope—a gentle sense that, even here, something good is still possible.
See, the practice of presence isn’t really about having the right technique. It’s more about being open—paying attention to the subtle ways God shows up. Sometimes it’s in beauty, sometimes in kindness, and sometimes in that still space between your thoughts. For some folks, that might mean prayer or meditation. For others, it could be a walk in nature, a moment with art, or even helping someone out.
There’s one woman who was pretty skeptical about religion. But she started practicing gratitude every evening, jotting down three things she was thankful for. At first, it was just an exercise. But over time, something shifted. She didn’t just feel better—she started noticing the sacred, quietly woven through her everyday life.
Here’s something to pay attention to: these practices aren’t about trying to earn God’s approval. They’re not about being perfect. It’s really just about making space for the possibility of encounter. Most of us don’t realize how easy it is to miss these moments. We get distracted by busyness, or weighed down by our worries. But when we slow down and pay attention, even the ordinary can suddenly feel meaningful.
In therapy, clients are often invited to experiment with these small practices. Not because they’re a magic fix, but as a gentle way to open up to God’s presence in their real, messy lives. And many people are surprised by what they find—a sense of peace, even when life is chaotic, a new way of seeing old problems, or a quiet joy that bubbles up for no obvious reason.
Over time, these little moments add up. They become the foundation for a faith that’s lived, not just believed. God’s presence stops being just an idea. It becomes something real—something you can lean on for comfort, guidance, and hope, no matter what you’re facing.
